title: Or nué
subtitle: Shaded couching over laid metal threads to create a coloured picture in gold
excerpt: Or nué lays pairs of gold passing threads across the fabric surface and couches them with coloured silk, placing the binding stitches close together where the design should appear dark and wide apart where the gold should gleam. The result is a shaded image that seems to glow from within.
sourceNotes: Barbara Dawson, Metal Thread Embroidery (1968), or nué chapter. Mrs Archibald Christie, Samplers and Stitches (1920), couched goldwork section. Royal School of Needlework standard goldwork curriculum as described in published manuals.

glossaryTerms.definition: A continuous metal thread made of a fine metal strip wound around a fibre core. It cannot be knotted or pierced by a needle and is always couched on the surface.
A metal laying and stroking tool used in goldwork to position threads, open loops, and ease metal threads into place without damaging them.

content.text: Or nué is a medieval goldwork technique in which the design is not drawn in gold but revealed by it. Pairs of
passing thread

are laid horizontally across the fabric in close parallel rows. A coloured silk thread couches each pair down, and by changing the spacing of those binding stitches, the embroiderer controls how much gold shows. Where binding stitches sit side by side, the silk covers the gold and creates solid colour. Where binding stitches are spread far apart, the gold shines through. The picture lives entirely in that adjustment of spacing.
What you need

items.label: Metal thread
items.value: Jap gold or fine gold passing thread, used in pairs

items.label: Couching thread
items.value: Silk thread in the design colours, waxed lightly with beeswax; one strand

items.label: Ground
items.value: Firm silk dupion or linen mounted over a layer of felt or flannel, stretched on a slate frame

items.label: Needle
items.value: Curved goldwork needle or large-eye needle for plunging thread ends; fine sharps needle size 10 for couching

content.text: Working the stitch
Transfer the design to the fabric. Stretch the ground fabric tightly on a slate frame so it cannot shift as you work.

Take a pair of passing threads and lay them horizontally across the full width of the design area. Hold the ends at the edge of the fabric with a small plunging needle or bend them back to be couched later. Use a
mellor
to keep the pair flat and side by side.

Thread a fine sharps needle with a single strand of silk in the colour needed at that point. Bring it up on one side of the gold pair and make a small right-angle binding stitch over both threads. Pull the stitch snug but do not drag the gold out of line.

Work across the row, adjusting spacing as the design dictates. In areas that should read as solid colour, place binding stitches touching or at 1 mm intervals. In areas where gold should show, open the spacing to 3 to 4 mm. Change silk colour within a row as the design requires, knotting off and starting a fresh colour without breaking the gold pair beneath.

At the end of the row, bend the gold pair back to start the next row immediately below. The rows must sit close together with no ground fabric showing between them. Continue filling the entire shape row by row.

When the shape is complete, take the cut ends of each gold pair to the back. Use the large-eye needle to pull them through. Secure them on the back of the ground with a few stitches of the waxed couching thread.
Common mistakes

items.symptom: The gold rows drift apart and the ground fabric shows between them
items.cause: Each new row was not laid immediately against the previous one.
items.fix: Use the mellor tip to nudge each new gold pair flush against the last row before you begin couching it.

items.symptom: The design image looks muddy rather than shaded
items.cause: The transition from close to open spacing is too abrupt, or the silk colours do not graduate in tone.
items.fix: Plan the spacing in stages: very close, half-close, alternating, sparse. Use a value study of the design before you begin. Work a small sample section first.

items.symptom: Passing thread kinks or curls at the turn
items.cause: The thread was bent at too sharp an angle at the end of a row.
items.fix: Ease the pair around a gentle curve at the selvedge using the mellor. A right-angle bend damages the metal; curve it softly instead.

content.text: Uses and related stitches
Or nué is closely related to
couching
and to
laid work
. It appears on medieval ecclesiastical embroidery such as the Syon Cope and remained the signature technique of the Flemish and Italian goldwork traditions.
